title: English Vocabulary in Use — Elementary · Units 21–22 (reviewed)
description: Units 21–22 reviewed against the illustrated teaching pages and exercises. Includes original example sentences, English usage notes, and British English IPA.
sourceNotice: Learning targets were selected with reference to the user-supplied book. Example sentences and explanatory notes are original; the exercises and illustrations are not reproduced.

audit.scope: Reviewed Unit 21 hotel diagrams, reception dialogue, service questions, and exercises 21.1–21.5; Unit 22 restaurant descriptions, illustrated menu, ordering dialogue, and exercises 22.1–22.6. Existing identifiers retained.
audit.pronunciation: British English IPA checked against the reference book phonemic index (PDF pages 160–170) for indexed forms; longer utterances were reviewed compositionally, without an independent pronunciation-dictionary check for each sentence.
audit.cannotGuarantee: Static checks cannot certify runtime import, speech synthesis, listening/pronunciation evaluation, adaptive review, or backup and restore. External phonetic verification and human editorial sign-off remain pending.

editorialReview.reviewMethod: Reviewed all original entries against teaching illustrations and exercises 21.1–21.5 and 22.1–22.6; cross-checked relevant headwords against the British phonemic index; ran local schema-like, ID, metadata, and English-only checks.
editorialReview.notes: Existing package, unit and item IDs were preserved. Browser importer, TTS, speaking/listening, learning progress, and backup/restore behaviour were not tested.

units.title: Unit 21 — In a hotel
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use Elementary, 3rd ed., Unit 21, printed pages 48–49 (PDF pages 49–50); original example sentences.
units.bookTitle: English Vocabulary in Use — Elementary (3rd edition)

items.section: A · Places and things in the hotel
items.example: Ask at reception for a city map.
items.note: The front-desk area of a hotel where guests check in and ask questions. Often used without the in at reception.

items.section: A · Places and things in the hotel
items.example: The receptionist gave us our room key.
items.note: The person who welcomes hotel guests and helps them at reception.

items.section: A · Places and things in the hotel
items.example: Take the lift to the third floor.
items.note: British English for the machine that carries people between floors; American English elevator.

items.section: A · Places and things in the hotel
items.example: Please complete this form before you go upstairs.
items.note: A document where you enter requested information. Fill in a form is a common phrase.

items.section: A · Places and things in the hotel
items.example: I left my room key at reception.
items.note: A room key opens the door to a hotel room.

items.section: A · Places and things in the hotel
items.example: Our room has a private bathroom.
items.note: A room with washing facilities. Do not confuse bathroom with bedroom.

items.section: A · Places and things in the hotel
items.example: There is a shower in the bathroom.
items.note: A shower can be the equipment or the activity. Say have a shower.

items.section: A · Places and things in the hotel
items.example: The TV in our room does not work.
items.note: Short for television; pronounced as the two letter names T and V.

items.section: A · Places and things in the hotel
items.example: There is a phone next to the bed.
items.note: Short for telephone. It can be a noun or a verb.

items.section: A · Places and things in the hotel
items.example: Could you help me with my luggage?
items.note: An uncountable noun for bags and suitcases; do not say luggages. Use a piece of luggage when counting.

items.section: A · Places and things in the hotel
items.example: Please check the bill before you pay.
items.note: A statement of charges you need to pay. You may ask to check your hotel bill.

items.section: A · Places and things in the hotel
items.example: We put the juice in the mini-bar.
items.note: A small hotel-room fridge or storage area containing drinks and snacks that may be charged separately.

items.section: A · Places and things in the hotel
items.example: Is there a hairdryer in the bathroom?
items.note: A device used to dry hair. Hair dryer is an alternative spelling.

items.example: I booked a single room for two nights.
items.note: In this context, a room intended for one person.

items.example: We need a double room for the weekend.
items.note: In the book, a room for two people; it does not always guarantee a double bed.

items.example: I have a reservation under the name Costa.
items.note: Tell the receptionist I have a reservation when you already booked a room.

items.example: Could you check my reservation?
items.note: A booking for a room or service, usually arranged before arrival.

items.example: We booked a room near the station.
items.note: Book is a verb meaning reserve something in advance, as in book a room.

items.example: I'd prefer a room with a view of the lake.
items.note: A room from which you can see an attractive place or landscape.

items.example: This room has a view of the sea.
items.note: Use a view of to describe what you can see from a hotel room. Sea means the ocean; see is a verb.

items.example: Our room is on the first floor.
items.note: In British English, the first floor is one floor above the ground floor; usage differs in American English.

items.example: The lift stops on the second floor.
items.note: In British English, the second floor is two levels above the ground floor; the phrase is reinforced in exercise 21.1.

items.example: Take the lift to your room.
items.note: The natural collocation for using a lift; also say go up or down in the lift.

items.example: The lift is over there, on your left.
items.note: Points to a place some distance from the speaker.

items.example: Can I help with your luggage?
items.note: Help with + noun is a useful pattern when offering or requesting assistance.

items.example: You need to fill in this form.
items.note: A separable phrasal verb meaning write required information in the spaces on a form.

items.example: Please sign here, next to your name.
items.note: Sign means write your signature or name. Here identifies the place on the form.

items.example: Check your bill for mistakes.
items.note: Check means look carefully to make sure the charges are correct.

items.example: Can we check out at midday?
items.note: To complete the departure process when leaving a hotel. The noun is check-out.

items.word: Can I have the bill, please?
items.pt: Pode trazer a conta, por favor?
items.example: Can I have the bill, please? We are leaving.
items.note: A polite request for the charges to pay. Could I have the bill, please? is also natural.

items.word: How much is a single room?
items.section: C · Asking questions about hotel services
items.example: How much is a single room for tonight?
items.note: Use How much is ...? to ask the price. Hotel prices may be per night.

items.section: C · Asking questions about hotel services
items.example: Room service is available until ten.
items.note: A hotel service that brings food or drinks to a guest’s room.

items.section: C · Asking questions about hotel services
items.example: Can I order room service now?
items.note: Order room service means request food or drinks to be brought to your room.

items.pt: linha externa (para ligar fora do hotel)
items.section: C · Asking questions about hotel services
items.example: I need an outside line to call my family.
items.note: A telephone connection to a number outside the hotel, especially on older hotel phone systems.

items.section: C · Asking questions about hotel services
items.example: How do I get an outside line?
items.note: A question about accessing external telephone calls from a hotel room.

items.section: C · Asking questions about hotel services
items.example: What's the country code for Japan?
items.note: A number used when calling a telephone number in another country; an explanatory extension of the source question.

items.section: C · Asking questions about hotel services
items.example: Do you know the code for Poland?
items.note: In a telephone context, code for + country asks for the international calling code.

items.section: C · Asking questions about hotel services
items.example: Can I have breakfast in my room?
items.note: A breakfast brought to or eaten in a guest’s room. Say have breakfast, not make breakfast, when eating it.

items.section: C · Asking questions about hotel services
items.example: I'd like a wake-up call at six.
items.note: A call arranged to wake a hotel guest at a specific time.

items.section: C · Asking questions about hotel services
items.example: Can I have a wake-up call at seven?
items.note: Use have a wake-up call at + time to request a call that wakes you.

items.pt: A que horas é o café da manhã?
items.section: C · Asking questions about hotel services
items.example: What time is breakfast on Sunday?
items.note: Ask about meal times. You can replace breakfast with lunch or dinner.

items.section: C · Asking questions about hotel services
items.example: Can I change money at reception?
items.note: Here, change means exchange one currency for another, not get coins as change after a purchase.

items.section: C · Asking questions about hotel services
items.example: Can I exchange euros for pounds here?
items.note: Exchange money means change one currency into another; exchange A for B is a common pattern.

items.pt: Posso fazer o check-out, por favor?
items.example: Can I check out, please? I have a train to catch.
items.note: A polite request made at reception when leaving a hotel.

items.word: Can I have a double room, please?
items.pt: Posso reservar um quarto para duas pessoas, por favor?
items.ipa: /kən aɪ hæv ə ˌdʌbəl ruːm pliːz/
items.example: Can I have a double room for two nights, please?
items.note: The request asks for a room for two people; for a particular bed arrangement, ask explicitly.

items.section: C · Asking questions about hotel services
items.example: We would like a room with a bathroom.
items.note: Use with + noun to specify a facility that a hotel room includes.

items.word: Can I have a wake-up call at six thirty, please?
items.pt: Posso receber uma ligação para despertar às seis e meia, por favor?
items.ipa: /kən aɪ hæv ə ˈweɪk ʌp kɔːl ət sɪks ˈθɜːti pliːz/
items.section: C · Asking questions about hotel services
items.example: Can I have a wake-up call at six thirty, please?
items.note: A complete request from the hotel-services dialogue, with a natural spoken time.

learningObjectives: Identify common hotel facilities, equipment, staff and their everyday uses.
Ask for a single or double room and specify a room with a view.
Explain a reservation, fill in and sign a form, check a bill, and check out.
Give and follow directions using the lift and floor numbers in British English.
Ask about room service, external calls, meal times, exchanging money and wake-up calls.

units.title: Unit 22 — Eating out
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use Elementary, 3rd ed., Unit 22, printed pages 50–51 (PDF pages 51–52); original example sentences.
units.bookTitle: English Vocabulary in Use — Elementary (3rd edition)

items.section: A · Places where you can eat
items.example: We stopped at a café for coffee and a sandwich.
items.note: A café is a place to buy drinks, snacks and sometimes meals. The accent is part of the common spelling.

items.section: A · Places where you can eat
items.example: We went to a small restaurant for dinner.
items.note: A place where you go to eat a meal; usually more formal than a café.

items.section: A · Places where you can eat
items.example: We met at a bar after work.
items.note: A place serving drinks, often with snacks or meals.

items.section: A · Places where you can eat
items.example: The pub serves lunch on Saturdays.
items.note: A public house, common in Britain, serving alcoholic and non-alcoholic drinks and often food.

items.section: A · Places where you can eat
items.example: We ate at a fast food restaurant.
items.note: A place serving meals that are prepared and provided quickly.

items.pt: comida para viagem; estabelecimento de retirada
items.section: A · Places where you can eat
items.example: We ordered dinner from a take-away.
items.note: British English for a place that sells food to take home, or the food itself; American English takeout.

items.section: A · Places where you can eat
items.example: We eat out once a week.
items.note: To eat a meal away from home, especially at a restaurant. Eating out appears in exercise 22.6.

items.section: A · Places where you can eat
items.example: That café also serves hot meals.
items.note: Breakfast, lunch and dinner are meals; a meal is not specifically lunch.

items.section: A · Places where you can eat
items.example: I had a snack between meetings.
items.note: A small amount of food eaten between or instead of regular meals.

items.section: A · Places where you can eat
items.example: This café serves meals in the evening.
items.note: A café, bar or pub may serve meals as well as drinks.

items.section: A · Places where you can eat
items.example: They do not serve alcohol here.
items.note: Alcohol here means alcoholic drinks; it is an uncountable noun in this sense.

items.section: A · Places where you can eat
items.example: Would you like a soft drink with your meal?
items.note: A non-alcoholic drink, often a fizzy drink. The broader category includes other non-alcoholic drinks.

items.section: A · Places where you can eat
items.example: I'd like some fruit juice.
items.note: Juice made from fruit; orange juice is a common example.

items.section: A · Places where you can eat
items.example: I had a cup of tea in the café.
items.note: The pattern a cup of + drink describes a serving in a cup.

items.section: A · Places where you can eat
items.example: She ordered a cheese sandwich.
items.note: Bread with a filling between slices or in a roll; a common café snack.

items.section: A · Places where you can eat
items.example: He had burger and chips for lunch.
items.note: A burger served with British chips, which are thick-cut fried potatoes; American English fries.

items.example: Could we see the menu, please?
items.note: A list of food and drinks that can be ordered in a restaurant.

items.example: I'll have soup as a starter.
items.note: The first, usually smaller, course of a meal. Often listed in the plural as Starters on menus.

items.example: The curry is my main course.
items.note: The principal dish in a meal. A menu may label the section Main courses.

items.example: Would you like a dessert?
items.note: A sweet dish eaten after the main course. Stress the second syllable; do not confuse it with desert.

items.example: The soup of the day is tomato.
items.note: A soup offered by the restaurant that day, often changing regularly.

items.example: We had chicken soup.
items.note: An uncountable food noun when referring to soup in general; order a bowl of soup.

items.example: I'd like tomato soup to start.
items.note: A type of soup made from tomatoes; one of the combinations reinforced in exercise 22.3.

items.example: Vegetable soup is my favourite starter.
items.note: Soup made with vegetables. It is a valid combination in exercise 22.3.

items.example: Chicken soup is good on cold days.
items.note: Soup made with chicken; another combination in exercise 22.3.

items.example: I'll have a mixed salad.
items.note: A salad containing several different ingredients. Listed as a vegetarian starter.

items.example: She ordered a tomato salad.
items.note: A salad containing tomatoes; reinforced in exercise 22.3.

items.example: We shared a fruit salad.
items.note: Pieces of several kinds of fruit; shown on the menu as a dessert.

items.example: My brother ordered a steak.
items.note: A piece of meat, usually beef. In the dialogue, the customer chooses how it is cooked.

items.example: I'd like steak with chips, please.
items.note: A main course of steak served with fried potatoes, described as chips in British English.

items.example: She chose new potatoes with her steak.
items.note: Small, newly harvested potatoes, often boiled and served as a side dish.

items.example: We had fish and chips by the sea.
items.note: A common British meal of fried fish, often battered, with chips.

items.example: The vegetable curry is delicious.
items.note: A spiced dish made with vegetables; listed as a vegetarian main course.

items.example: I often cook chicken curry.
items.note: A curry made with chicken; reinforced in exercise 22.3.

items.example: The restaurant serves beef curry.
items.note: A curry made with beef; reinforced in exercise 22.3.

items.example: I ordered a salmon fillet.
items.note: A piece of salmon without the bones; the first l in salmon is silent.

items.example: The fish comes with green beans.
items.note: Long green vegetables often served cooked as a side dish.

items.example: There are mushrooms in the burger.
items.note: The plural of mushroom; a type of edible fungus and a common savoury ingredient.

items.example: I'd like chocolate ice cream for dessert.
items.note: Ice cream flavoured with chocolate; listed as a dessert.

items.example: We shared an apple pie.
items.note: A baked dessert with apples inside pastry.

items.example: I ordered a chicken pie.
items.note: A savoury pie with chicken; the combination is reinforced in exercise 22.3.

items.example: Is this curry vegetarian?
items.note: A vegetarian does not eat meat or fish; (v) on the menu marks vegetarian options.

items.example: The waiter brought our drinks.
items.note: A person who takes orders and serves customers in a restaurant.

items.pt: Já escolheram?; Estão prontos para pedir?
items.example: Are you ready to order, or do you need a minute?
items.note: A common question from a waiter when asking whether customers have decided what to eat.

items.example: I'd like the vegetable soup, please.
items.note: A polite pattern for ordering. Replace the ellipsis with a dish or drink in speech.

items.example: Would you like the steak with chips or new potatoes?
items.note: A polite question offering someone a choice. Complete the question with the item or action.

items.word: How would you like your steak?
items.pt: Como você quer o ponto do bife?
items.example: How would you like your steak: rare, medium or well-done?
items.note: The waiter is asking how well the steak should be cooked.

items.example: I prefer my steak rare.
items.note: For steak, cooked briefly so the inside remains red. Here rare does not mean uncommon.

items.example: She asked for her steak medium.
items.note: For steak, cooked between rare and well-done, typically still pink in the centre.

items.example: He always eats his steak well-done.
items.note: For steak, cooked until no red remains inside. As an adjective before a noun, well-done is hyphenated.

items.word: What would you like to drink?
items.pt: O que você gostaria de beber?
items.example: What would you like to drink with your meal?
items.note: A polite way to ask which drink someone wants.

items.example: I'll have an orange juice, please.
items.note: A natural expression for choosing a dish or drink in a restaurant. Replace the ellipsis in speech.

items.example: Is everything all right with your meal?
items.note: A polite check by a waiter asking whether the meal and service are satisfactory.

items.example: The soup is delicious.
items.note: An adjective meaning that food or drink tastes very good.

items.word: Could I have the bill, please?
items.pt: Pode trazer a conta, por favor?
items.example: Could I have the bill, please?
items.note: A polite request to pay after a meal. In British English, bill is usual; American English also uses check.

items.example: Of course, I'll bring it now.
items.note: An affirmative, polite reply meaning certainly or yes.

items.section: A · Places where you can eat
items.example: Could I have a cup of coffee, please?
items.note: In a café, a cup of coffee is a common way to order a serving of coffee.

items.section: A · Places where you can eat
items.example: She ordered a small piece of cake with her coffee.
items.note: A common café snack; a piece or slice of cake refers to one serving.

items.section: A · Places where you can eat
items.example: I would like chips with my burger.
items.note: In British English, chips are pieces of fried potato; American English usually calls these fries.

items.section: A · Places where you can eat
items.example: We usually have lunch at twelve thirty.
items.note: Lunch is the meal in the middle of the day; have lunch is the usual pattern.

items.section: A · Places where you can eat
items.example: They are having dinner at a restaurant tonight.
items.note: Dinner is commonly the main meal in the evening, although usage varies.

items.example: I will have a coke with my meal.
items.note: A common informal word for a cola drink; the customer orders one in the dialogue.

items.word: Would you like it with chips or new potatoes?
items.pt: Você gostaria de acompanhar com batatas fritas ou batatas novas?
items.ipa: /wʊd ju laɪk ɪt wɪð tʃɪps ɔː njuː pəˈteɪtəʊz/
items.example: Would you like it with chips or new potatoes?
items.note: Use with + side dish when offering accompaniments to a main course.

learningObjectives: Distinguish cafés, restaurants, pubs, bars, fast food restaurants and take-aways.
Read a menu and identify starters, main courses, desserts and vegetarian dishes.
Use common food collocations for soups, salads, curries, steak, pie and side dishes.
Order food and drinks politely with I’d like, I’ll have and Would you like.
Describe how steak is cooked and ask for the bill using natural restaurant expressions.
